GitHub Actions OIDC Trust Policy Checker

Paste an AWS IAM role trust policy and find out whether its conditions actually restrict which repository, branch or environment can assume the role. The common failures are quiet ones: a policy that pins aud and leaves sub unconstrained is assumable by any repository on GitHub; repo:my-org/my-repo:* admits the pull_request context and therefore a fork's pull request; and a * under StringEquals is a literal character, so the role cannot be assumed at all. Each of those looks approximately correct in a policy review.

Nothing is uploaded. Your policy is parsed here, in your browser. That matters more than usual for this input: a trust policy carries your AWS account id, your role name and your repository names.

Already run Wiz or a comparable CNAPP across your cloud account? See this checker vs. Wiz for when each is the right one to reach for. Just reading the policy JSON yourself? See this checker vs. reading the trust policy by eye for what a manual read catches and what it misses.

Paste your trust policy

In the console: IAM → Roles → your role → Trust relationships. Or on the command line — this is the whole document, and the command needs only read access: 

aws iam get-role --role-name my-deploy-role --query Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument

Paste the trust policy above and click Check.

Report

Run it in CI instead

The same classifier ships as a zero-dependency Node.js CLI, so a pull request that widens a trust policy can fail a check rather than being noticed later. It makes no network request and needs no AWS credentials — it reads a file and exits, so it runs offline: 

node check.mjs trust-policy.json
# or straight from the AWS CLI:
aws iam get-role --role-name my-deploy-role \
  --query Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument | node check.mjs -

Exit code 0 when no danger-level finding is present, 1 when there is one — so it works as a gate as it stands. Get check.mjs and analyze.mjs from the repo.

What the sub claim looks like

Every pattern this tool reasons about comes from the shape of GitHub's sub claim. In its default form it is repo:<owner>/<repo>:<context>, and the context is the part that decides whether a stranger's pull request is included:

ref:refs/heads/maina push or workflow run on that branch
ref:refs/tags/v1.2.3a workflow run for that tag
environment:productiona job targeting that environment — the one context that can carry required reviewers
pull_requesta workflow triggered by a pull request, including one opened from a fork

An organisation can customise which claims the issuer includes, in which case a policy written against it will legitimately not match this shape — the report says so rather than guessing. The longer walkthrough of these traps works through each one with the policy that produces it.

Common questions

My trust policy pins the aud claim to sts.amazonaws.com. Isn't that enough?

No, and this is the most expensive misreading of this policy shape. Every AWS and GitHub Actions OIDC integration in the world uses the audience sts.amazonaws.com — it identifies which service the token is for, not which repository issued it. A policy that pins aud and leaves sub unconstrained is assumable by a GitHub Actions workflow in any repository on GitHub. Pinning aud is necessary and it is not isolation; the sub claim is the only condition that says which repository.

What is wrong with sub set to repo:my-org/my-repo:*?

It pins the repository but not the context, and GitHub's sub claim carries the context in that final segment. So the pattern matches every branch, every tag, every environment — and repo:my-org/my-repo:pull_request, which GitHub issues to workflows triggered by a pull request. On a public repository, or any repository that accepts forks, that means someone with no write access can open a pull request and have its workflow assume your role. Pin a ref (repo:owner/name:ref:refs/heads/main) or an environment instead.

Why does a wildcard under StringEquals show up as a notice rather than a danger?

Because IAM only treats * and ? as wildcards under the StringLike family of operators. Under StringEquals they are ordinary characters, so a condition of StringEquals sub = repo:org/name:* is asking for a sub claim whose last character is literally an asterisk. No GitHub token ever carries that, so the condition never matches and the role cannot be assumed at all. That fails closed: it is a broken deployment, not an exposure, and a checker that reported it as an open wildcard would send you to fix the opposite of the real problem.

I listed four pinned branches in my sub condition. Why is it still flagged?

IAM grants access when any one value in the list matches, so a multi-value sub condition is exactly as permissive as its widest entry. Four tightly pinned branches plus one repo:org/name:* is as open as the wildcard alone, and reading the list from the top finds the four good rows first. This tool reports which entry actually governs rather than the first one it sees.

Does this send my trust policy anywhere?

No. The page parses and classifies the policy in your own browser using JavaScript loaded from this site, and makes no network request with the content. That matters here more than usual: a trust policy contains your AWS account id, your role name, and the names of your repositories. The Node.js CLI is the same code and also makes no network request of any kind — it reads a file and exits, so it needs no AWS credentials and works offline.

Does a clean report mean my OIDC setup is secure?

No. This reads the trust policy only — the door, not the room behind it. It cannot see what permissions the role grants once assumed, who can push to the branch you pinned, whether a protected environment actually has reviewers configured, or whether your organisation has customised the OIDC subject claim. A role correctly pinned to a branch that any contributor can push to is still reachable by any contributor. Treat a clean report as evidence about these specific conditions, not a determination that the setup is secure.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks a specific set of documented conditions on one trust policy. It is not a full security assessment, cannot see the permissions the role grants once assumed, cannot see who is able to push to a branch you have pinned, and cannot see a pattern it does not check for. A clean report describes what these conditions say, not a guarantee that the setup is secure.

Nothing leaves your browser. The policy you paste is parsed and classified on this page by JavaScript served from this site; it is never uploaded, and no request carries it anywhere. That is deliberate — a trust policy names your AWS account, your role and your repositories. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used and the day: no policies, no account ids, no repository names, no account, no tracking cookies, no analytics vendor. Turn it off with the checkbox above.

sub-claim-and-wildcard-traps.html.text:
Why repo:my-org/my-repo:* lets a stranger's pull request into your AWS account

Federating GitHub Actions into AWS with OIDC is the right move: it replaces a long-lived AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in your repository secrets with a short-lived token minted per run. The catch is that the entire security boundary then lives in one place — the role's trust policy — and the ways that document goes wrong all look approximately correct while you are reading it.

The sub claim is the only thing that says "which repository"

When a workflow requests a token, GitHub signs a set of claims about the run. Two of them appear in almost every trust policy, and they do very different jobs:

aud The audience — sts.amazonaws.com. This is the same value for every AWS/GitHub OIDC integration on the planet. It says the token is meant for AWS STS. It says nothing whatsoever about who issued it.
sub The subject — repo:<owner>/<repo>:<context>. This is the only claim that identifies the repository and the circumstances of the run.

So a trust policy that carefully pins aud and says nothing about sub is assumable by a GitHub Actions workflow in any repository on GitHub. Anyone can create a repository, add a workflow, and request a token with that audience. This is the single highest-severity version of the mistake, and it is easy to ship because the policy visibly contains a condition block and visibly names GitHub's issuer.

The context segment decides whether forks are included

The context is the part after the repository, and it is one of:

ref:refs/heads/maina run on that branch
ref:refs/tags/v1.2.3a run for that tag
environment:productiona job targeting that environment — the only context that can carry required reviewers
pull_requesta run triggered by a pull request, including one opened from a fork

Which is why repo:my-org/my-repo:* is not the harmless "just this repo" shorthand it looks like. It matches all four rows. On a public repository — or any repository that accepts pull requests from forks — that includes a workflow run proposed by someone with no write access and no review. If the role can write to production, so can they. 

// Looks locked down. Is not.
"Condition": {
  "StringEquals": { "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com" },
  "StringLike":   { "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:my-org/my-repo:*" }
}

The fix is to name the context you actually deploy from:

"Condition": {
  "StringEquals": {
    "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
    "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:my-org/my-repo:ref:refs/heads/main"
  }
}

Note that this uses StringEquals, not StringLike. When you are pinning an exact value, an equality operator is both clearer and immune to a wildcard sneaking in later.

The trap that runs the other way: a literal asterisk

IAM only treats * and ? as wildcards under the StringLike family of operators. Under StringEquals they are ordinary characters. So this: 

"StringEquals": { "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:my-org/my-repo:*" }

is asking for a subject claim whose last character is literally an asterisk. No GitHub token ever carries one, so the condition never matches and the role cannot be assumed at all. This fails closed. It is a broken deployment pipeline, not an exposure — and it is worth calling out separately, because a checker that reports it as "wildcard in sub: critical" sends you to tighten a policy that is already refusing everybody, while the actual symptom is a deploy job failing with an unhelpful STS error.

In a list of values, the widest one wins

IAM grants access when any value in a condition list matches. So a policy like this is exactly as permissive as its last line, no matter how carefully the first three are written: 

"StringLike": {
  "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": [
    "repo:my-org/my-repo:ref:refs/heads/main",
    "repo:my-org/my-repo:ref:refs/heads/staging",
    "repo:my-org/my-repo:environment:production",
    "repo:my-org/my-repo:*"
  ]
}

Read top-down, that list is reassuring for three lines. This is a common shape in practice because entries get appended over time — someone adds a temporary wildcard to unblock a release and it stays.

One more: a negated operator does not pin anything

StringNotEquals and StringNotLike exclude what they list and permit everything else. A condition that excludes one repository still admits every other repository on GitHub, so a negated operator on sub is not a narrower pin — it is an open door with one name struck off.

What this does not cover

The trust policy is the door, not the room. Even a perfectly pinned policy leaves questions it cannot answer: what the role is permitted to do once assumed, who can push to the branch you pinned, and whether the environment you named actually has required reviewers configured. A role pinned to ref:refs/heads/main in a repository where any contributor can push to main is reachable by any contributor. And an organisation can customise which claims its OIDC issuer includes, in which case a policy written against the customised claim will legitimately not match the default shape described here.

This is evidence about a specific set of conditions, not a full security assessment — see the checker and its disclaimer for what it does and doesn't cover. The checker applies every rule on this page to a policy you paste, in your browser, with nothing uploaded, and ships the same classifier as a zero-dependency CLI you can run as a CI gate.

vs-reading-the-trust-policy-by-eye.html.text:
← OIDC Trust Policy Check

This checker vs. reading the trust policy by eye

The free way to review a GitHub Actions OIDC trust policy is to open the JSON and read the Condition block: does sub look pinned, is there an obvious * sitting somewhere it shouldn't. That catches the case where nothing at all restricts the role, and costs nothing but a few minutes of careful reading.

This checker runs the same read, but resolves every statement against IAM's actual condition-operator semantics before judging it -- rather than treating a trailing * as always meaning the same thing. A sub value under StringLike is a real wildcard; the identical string under StringEquals is a literal character that no real GitHub token can match, and reporting it as an exposure would send the reader to fix a role that is actually failing closed. It also checks aud against the one audience every GitHub/AWS OIDC integration actually uses, walks every value in a multi-value condition rather than stopping at the first tightly-scoped one, and flags a repo:org/name:* pattern for including pull_request -- a context GitHub issues to fork-triggered workflows opened by strangers.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Spot-check a trust policy you just wrote for an obvious, unconditioned *. Reading it by eye -- fast, and good enough to catch the plainest case.
Know whether a sub value ending in * is a real wildcard or a literal character that fails closed, without holding IAM's operator semantics in your head. This checker -- it resolves each statement's actual condition operator automatically.
Confirm aud being pinned actually restricts who can assume the role. This checker -- it names the one audience every real OIDC integration uses, so a pinned aud alone is never read as isolation.
Check every value in a multi-value sub condition, not just the first few tightly-scoped ones. This checker -- it walks the whole list, since IAM treats it as "any of these match."
Notice that a repo:org/name:* pattern is assumable from a fork's pull request, not just from branches in the same repository. This checker -- it names the pull_request exposure explicitly.
Gate a policy change in CI without a human review step every time. This checker -- one Node command, no AWS credentials, a machine-checkable pass/fail.

A careful read is a reasonable first pass, and it is often what catches the policy with nothing at all in its Condition block. This checker is what you run once the policy has a condition that looks right -- it resolves the operator semantics a human reviewer would otherwise have to memorise, per statement, every time.

Common questions

Isn't scanning the trust policy for a wildcard enough?

It catches the obvious case -- a bare * with no condition operator narrowing it at all. What it does not catch is the operator-dependent reading: a sub value of repo:org/name:* under StringLike is a genuine wildcard covering every branch, tag, and pull request in that repository, while the exact same string under StringEquals is a literal character match that no real GitHub token will ever satisfy -- it fails closed rather than opening anything. A reviewer has to hold that distinction in mind for every statement in the policy; this checker applies it automatically and reports which one each statement actually is.

What does a manual read of the policy tend to miss?

Three shapes in particular. First, the operator-dependent wildcard above. Second, aud being mistaken for identity: every AWS/GitHub OIDC integration uses the same audience, sts.amazonaws.com, so a policy that pins aud tightly but leaves sub unconstrained reads as locked down while being assumable by any repository on GitHub -- pinning aud is necessary and is not, by itself, isolation. Third, a multi-value sub condition: IAM treats a list of values as "any of these match," so four tightly scoped branches plus one repo:org/name:* entry are exactly as open as the wildcard alone, and a top-to-bottom read tends to find the four good rows first and stop looking.

Why does repo:org/name:* matter for pull_request specifically?

Because GitHub issues that sub claim shape to workflows triggered by a pull_request event, including one opened from a fork by someone with no write access to the repository. A policy scoped to that pattern is assumable by a stranger's pull request, not just by trusted branches in the same repo -- a detail that is easy to miss when eyeballing a condition block that otherwise looks like a normal repo-and-branch restriction.

Is anything I paste into either process uploaded?

There is nothing to upload either way. Reading a trust policy JSON file in a review tool or an editor involves no third party by itself, and this checker's browser page only parses and classifies the JSON you paste in locally -- a trust policy names your AWS account, your role, and your repositories, so nothing about it is sent anywhere. The CLI reads a file from your own disk and makes no network request either.

Evidence, not a determination. This checker classifies documented condition patterns on one trust policy. It is not a full security assessment, cannot see the permissions the role grants once assumed, and cannot see a pattern it does not check for. A clean report describes what these conditions say, not a guarantee that the setup is secure.

vs-wiz.html.text:
← GitHub Actions OIDC Trust Policy Checker

This checker vs. Wiz

Two different layers: Wiz continuously inventories a whole cloud account's IAM roles and trust relationships, alongside dozens of other cloud risk categories, as part of a paid platform. This tool reads one pasted trust policy's GitHub Actions OIDC conditions, once, locally — no account, no cloud connection, nothing installed.

What each product is for

Wiz is a cloud-native application protection platform (CNAPP). Per its own public material, it connects agentlessly to a customer's AWS, Azure, GCP, or other cloud accounts and builds a graph correlating roles, permissions, workloads, data, vulnerabilities, and exposed secrets across the whole environment, surfacing risks such as over-permissive IAM trust policies as one of many finding types. Wiz's own security research team has published specifically on GitHub Actions OIDC trust-policy misconfigurations — a missing or wildcarded sub condition letting an unintended repository assume a role — as one instance of the broader IAM risk category its platform inventories continuously. Wiz publishes no public price list on its own site, so no dollar figure for it is stated here as verified fact; only its well-documented product category (an enterprise, account-connected CNAPP) is described.

This tool does none of what Wiz does. It connects to no cloud account, runs no agent, and holds no ongoing inventory of anything. You paste one AWS IAM role trust policy — the one federating GitHub Actions over OIDC — and it classifies that policy's sub and aud conditions against the specific wildcard-scope and operator-semantics traps this misconfiguration class is known for: no sub condition at all, a wildcard reaching past one repository, repo:owner/name:* admitting a fork's pull request, a negated operator, a missing or wildcarded aud, and a literal * under StringEquals that makes the role unassumable rather than open. It runs free in your browser (or as a zero-dependency CLI), with nothing uploaded and no network calls of its own.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want continuous, account-wide inventory of every IAM role's trust relationships, correlated against workloads, secrets, and vulnerabilities — not just one GitHub Actions role.Wiz, or a comparable CNAPP — that is the ongoing, cross-account job it is built for.
I just wrote (or inherited) one AWS IAM role trust policy for GitHub Actions OIDC and want to know right now whether its sub/aud conditions actually pin it to my repo.This tool — paste the policy, get the findings, free, no account.
I want an agent or connected account that watches my whole cloud estate for new over-permissive roles as they're created.Wiz — this tool has no memory between runs and connects to nothing.
I don't want to connect a cloud account or install anything to check one trust policy that names my own AWS account id.This tool — it never makes a network call, and nothing you paste is uploaded.
I want correlated findings across IAM, secrets, vulnerabilities, and data exposure in one graph.Wiz — this tool checks one narrow, specific misconfiguration class and nothing else.
What exactly is the sub/wildcard trap, and how do I fix it?This tool's own sub-claim and wildcard traps explainer.

A team can reasonably use both: Wiz for continuous, account-wide cloud security posture management, and this tool as a fast, zero-account, zero-network check of one trust policy's OIDC conditions the moment it's written. This page does not evaluate Wiz's detection accuracy or coverage and makes no claim about it either way — it only describes Wiz's documented product category and states what this tool does differently. A clean result from either one is not a complete security assessment on its own.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the check runs in your browser (or as a stdlib-only CLI script), and it keeps working with the network connection off.

Common questions

Does Wiz check GitHub Actions OIDC trust policy conditions the same way this tool does?

Not in the way this tool does. Wiz is a cloud-native application protection platform (CNAPP): per its own public material, it connects to a customer's cloud accounts (AWS, Azure, GCP and others) and continuously maps relationships across every role, permission, and resource to surface risks such as over-permissive trust policies, alongside a broad range of other cloud misconfigurations, vulnerabilities and exposed secrets. Wiz's own security research team has specifically written about the exact class of bug this tool checks for -- a GitHub Actions OIDC trust policy whose sub condition is missing or too broad, letting an unintended repository assume the role -- as one finding among the many categories its platform inventories across a whole account. This tool does the opposite and narrower thing: it makes no connection to any cloud account and holds no ongoing inventory. You paste one IAM role trust policy, and it classifies that policy's sub and aud conditions against the specific wildcard and operator-semantics traps documented for this exact misconfiguration, entirely offline.

Should I use this tool or Wiz?

They work at different layers, and a team can reasonably use both. Wiz connects to a cloud account on an ongoing, agentless basis and correlates findings across IAM, workloads, data, and vulnerabilities into one graph, as part of a paid enterprise platform; no public price list exists on Wiz's own site, so no dollar figure is stated here as verified fact. This tool needs no cloud account connection, no agent, and no ongoing subscription: paste one trust policy and get its sub/aud conditions classified in your browser, free, in under a second, with nothing uploaded. A platform team standardizing least-privilege across every role in a large cloud estate is better served by Wiz or a comparable CNAPP; a developer wiring up one new GitHub Actions OIDC role right now, who wants an immediate, free, local answer to whether its trust policy is scoped correctly, is in the right place here.

No. This page is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Wiz, Inc. Wiz is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this tool is and is not, based on Wiz's own publicly documented product and research.

Open the GitHub Actions OIDC Trust Policy Checker to check your own policy, or read sub-claim and wildcard traps for the full mechanism.
